overview: Struthiomimus altus ("ostrich mimic") was a large ornithomimosaur from the Campanian of Alberta (~75 Ma), reaching about 4.2 metres. As one of the better-known ornithomimosaurs, it has been at the centre of debates about the diet of these toothless, long-legged theropods — with hypotheses ranging from insectivory to herbivory to filter-feeding depending on the era of analysis.

Current understanding, informed by bone microstructure, jaw mechanics and ecological comparisons, favours an omnivorous diet similar to modern ratite birds: plant material, insects, small vertebrates and occasional carrion. Struthiomimus was fast — likely capable of 50+ km/h — and this speed was its primary defence in a fauna that included the large tyrannosaur Gorgosaurus.

fossilSites.name: Dinosaur Park Formation
fossilSites.note: Campanian floodplain deposits with multiple Struthiomimus specimens and the richest Late Cretaceous dinosaur fauna known from North America.

articles.title: Discovery and naming
articles.body: Described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1917 from Dinosaur Park Formation material collected by Barnum Brown. The name "ostrich mimic" reflects its superficially ostrich-like proportions. It is one of the most abundant large theropods in its formation, suggesting it was a successful member of the Campanian coastal plain fauna.

articles.title: Locomotion and speed
articles.body: Ornithomimosaur hindlimb proportions — the ratio of tibia to femur length and metatarsal length — are among the most bird-like of any non-avian dinosaur. Computer modelling based on muscle mass and limb geometry suggests top speeds of 50–60 km/h for large adults. The tail was held stiffly horizontal as a counterbalance, and the arms were long and strong, probably used for foraging rather than prey capture.

articles.title: Diet debate
articles.body: The absence of teeth and the beak morphology have made ornithomimosaur diet contentious. Filter-feeding (water-straining like flamingos) was proposed based on apparent comb-like structures in one specimen's beak — later reinterpreted as preservational artefacts. Jaw mechanics, gut contents and ecological modelling now support omnivory: plant material, insects, small vertebrates and possibly eggs.

fossilRecord.material: Multiple articulated skeletons documenting a long-limbed ornithomimid.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous coastal plain of Alberta alongside Albertosaurus and Edmontosaurus.
fossilRecord.evidence: A long-limbed, toothless-beaked skeleton supports fast locomotion and an omnivorous diet; direct feather/quill-knob evidence comes from its close relative Ornithomimus, with a similar covering inferred for Struthiomimus by phylogenetic bracketing.

record.mya: late Campanian, about 77-75 million years ago
record.description: Struthiomimus altus was an ornithomimid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, known from several partial skeletons including well-preserved limbs and hands.
facts: Long hindlimbs support rapid bipedal locomotion, but no exact top speed can be recovered.
Its toothless beak does not identify a single diet; herbivory and omnivory remain alternatives.

presentation.heroLead: A long-legged, toothless ostrich-mimic theropod from Late Cretaceous Alberta, known from one famous articulated skeleton and several partial ones.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Struthiomimus altus
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Struthiomimus altus, a slender, long-necked, feathered theropod with long legs and a small toothless head, in side view
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration based on a published skeletal reconstruction. The feathery covering is inferred from related ornithomimids; colour and the exact extent of plumage are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Struthiomimus was a lightly built theropod about four metres long with a small, toothless, beaked head on a long neck, slender arms ending in three long-clawed fingers, and long, powerful hindlimbs. Its name means ostrich mimic, and the body proportions really are close to those of a large flightless bird with a long tail added.

The best specimen, AMNH 5339, was found on the Red Deer River in 1914 with the skeleton still articulated in a death pose, which is why the proportions of Struthiomimus are known more securely than for most ornithomimids. Other skeletons from the same rocks are partial, and the skull is less well preserved than the rest of the body.

The beak and grasping hands have been read in several ways, from browsing on plants and filtering water to catching small animals. None of these is confirmed by gut contents, so the diet remains open, with a plant-rich or mixed diet the most commonly favoured options.
animalHighlights: Ostrich-like proportions with long legs and a slender neck are documented directly in an articulated skeleton.
The toothless beak and three long, nearly equal fingers with weakly curved claws are unusual among theropods.
The hindlimb is built for speed, although no top speed can be measured from the bones.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Beak and hands allow several diets
lifeCards.reason: A toothless beak and clawed hands are consistent with browsing, omnivory or small-prey capture. No gut contents or wear evidence settles the question.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Long, slender hindlimbs and a compact foot indicate a fast two-legged animal; an exact speed cannot be calculated from the skeleton.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: The articulated skeleton gives length directly. Mass estimates of around 150 kilograms are model-based and vary between authors.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: No integument is preserved in Struthiomimus; feather evidence comes from the closely related Ornithomimus.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Red Deer River valley, Alberta, Canada

locality.name: Red Deer River valley
locality.note: Dinosaur Park Formation, in and around what is now Dinosaur Provincial Park. Lambe's original type material and the articulated AMNH skeleton both come from this stretch of the river.

presentation.classificationSummary: Struthiomimus is an ornithomimid, one of the toothless ostrich-mimic theropods within Coelurosauria. It is closely related to Ornithomimus from the same rocks, and telling the two apart from partial material remains a recurring problem.

related.reason: Compare with the closely related Alberta ornithomimid that preserves feather evidence.
Compare with a larger Mongolian ornithomimid known from many skeletons.
Compare with a giant, deep-bodied ornithomimosaur that shows how varied the group became.

questions.title: What did it eat?
questions.copy: The beak does not identify a diet. Suggestions range from plants and small animals to filter-feeding, and the hands have been compared with those of sloths and birds. No direct evidence exists.

questions.title: Which bones are really Struthiomimus?
questions.copy: Ornithomimus lived in the same rocks and looks similar. Partial skeletons and material from other formations have been moved between the two genera more than once.

questions.title: How fast could it run?
questions.copy: The hindlimb is clearly built for speed, but published speed figures are extrapolations from limb proportions rather than measurements.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.note: Partial pelvis and hindlimb from the Red Deer River, named by Lambe in 1902 as Ornithomimus altus.

specimens.name: Referred articulated skeleton
specimens.institution: American Museum of Natural History, New York
specimens.note: Near-complete postcranial skeleton with damaged skull collected by Barnum Brown in 1914; the basis of Osborn's 1917 genus description.

panel.headline: One articulated skeleton and several partial ones from Alberta.
panel.standfirst: Struthiomimus altus is anchored by Lambe's partial pelvis and hindlimb and is best known from AMNH 5339, an articulated skeleton collected by Barnum Brown in 1914, supplemented by other partial skeletons from the Dinosaur Park Formation.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: The postcranial skeleton is well documented, chiefly from one articulated individual, but the skull is incompletely known and few other individuals are substantially complete.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: AMNH 5339 preserves the vertebral column, girdles, both forelimbs with hands and both hindlimbs in articulation, with a damaged skull. The holotype and further referred specimens add pelvic, limb and hand material from other individuals in the same formation.
knownRemains.note: Because so much rests on one skeleton, individual and growth variation are hard to assess, and specimens from outside the Dinosaur Park Formation are not securely assigned.

media.title: AMNH 5339 as figured by Osborn in 1917
media.alt: Photograph plate of the articulated Struthiomimus altus skeleton AMNH 5339 lying in its rock slab with the neck arched back
media.caption: The articulated skeleton collected by Barnum Brown in 1914 on the Red Deer River, as published in Osborn's 1917 description of the genus. The neck is drawn back in a typical death pose.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A crushed, incomplete skull with toothless jaws in AMNH 5339; cranial material is otherwise scarce.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Articulated neck, back, sacrum and tail in AMNH 5339, with ribs and gastralia.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Shoulder and pelvic girdles and complete forelimbs and hindlimbs, including well-preserved hands, from AMNH 5339 and other partial skeletons; the holotype is a partial pelvis and hindlimb.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Articulation of AMNH 5339 preserves natural proportions. No skin, feathers or gut contents are known for the genus.

specimenCards.title: CMN 930 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial pelvis with hindlimb elements from the Red Deer River, named Ornithomimus altus by Lawrence Lambe in 1902 and made the type of the new genus Struthiomimus by Osborn in 1917.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River, Alberta · Dinosaur Park Formation · Canadian Museum of Nature, Ottawa

specimenCards.title: AMNH 5339 · articulated skeleton
specimenCards.description: A near-complete postcranial skeleton with damaged skull found by Barnum Brown in 1914. It supplied most of what is known about the proportions and hands of Struthiomimus and anchored Osborn's description of the genus.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River, Alberta · Dinosaur Park Formation · American Museum of Natural History, New York

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: An articulated postcranial skeleton with hands and feet, a damaged toothless skull, and partial pelvic and limb material from further individuals.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: Limb proportions indicate a fast biped; the beak and hand form permit plant-eating, omnivory or small-prey capture; feathers are inferred from the related Ornithomimus.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Diet, detailed skull anatomy, growth and individual variation, integument, and which partial skeletons from other formations belong to the genus.
